The cup behind the flowerpot

Ella cannot find her small blue cup. She looks on the kitchen table and beside the sink, but it is not there. Her brother asks whether she took it into the garden. Ella remembers drinking water while drawing flowers. They go outside together. The cup is behind a flowerpot, where she put it to keep the paper dry. A tiny leaf has fallen inside. Ella takes the cup back to the kitchen and washes it before using it again. Her brother says the cup had a garden adventure. Ella writes a reminder beside her drawing: bring the things you need back inside.

originalGroup.material:
A bridge for the toy bus

Tom makes a paper bridge for his toy bus. He puts one end on a low box and the other on a stack of books. At first, the middle bends and the bus stops. His sister folds another sheet like a fan and puts it under the bridge. The folded paper helps support the middle. Tom tries again, and the bus crosses slowly. He does not put his feet on the little bridge; it is made for a toy. After playing, he keeps a drawing of the folds. The next day, he wants to try the same idea with a lighter model car.

originalGroup.material:
A number on the thermostat

A thermostat can display a temperature as a ____1____, but that figure may refer to the room's current temperature or to the temperature the user wants. Understanding which one is shown matters before deciding that the system is working incorrectly.

A ____2____ detects temperature at a particular point. The controller can use a ____3____ between the detected value and the desired one to determine a heating action. The exact behaviour depends on the equipment and how it has been arranged.

The system's ____4____ is not necessarily instant. Heat takes time to move through a room, and a displayed change does not mean every corner becomes warm ____5____. Turning a control repeatedly may therefore create confusion if the user expects the air to follow each movement at once.

A person may ____6____ the desired temperature, but the effect still depends on the building and heating system. The change in the room can be ____7____ rather than sudden. A number on a display is an instruction or observation within a process, not a magic description of everything in the room.

The device's ____8____ also matters. A reading near one source of warmth may differ from conditions elsewhere. That does not automatically prove the instrument is broken. It may show that one measurement point does not represent every place equally.

Useful controls combine readable information with a ____9____ relation between what users do and what the system does. Instructions should explain the relevant limits instead of relying on the user to guess. Knowing those limits helps people make a considered adjustment rather than operate the control ____10____.

originalGroup.material:
The work a typeface is asked to do

A typeface can be chosen for its personality, but a reading page also asks it to perform practical work. One concern is ____1____: whether individual letters and words can be recognised under the conditions in which they will be read. An attractive sample does not answer that question for every use.

Readers need to ____2____ similar forms. A design that looks elegant in a large heading may make some characters harder to tell apart in a small label. Size, spacing and the medium all contribute to the result.

The relevant ____3____ is therefore more than the font's name. A long printed essay, a moving display and a short interface label make different demands. Testing only a decorative title gives limited information about sustained reading.

Some ____4____ within the design can support recognition. If every form were made nearly identical for visual neatness, readers would lose useful differences. Consistency need not mean erasing every distinctive feature.

A page also uses type to establish a ____5____. Headings, notes and body text can signal different roles. The point is to make those relationships apparent, not simply multiply styles. Too many competing signals can make the structure less clear.

Design choices have ____6____ for different readers. A difficult page may discourage someone even when every sentence is technically present. It is unhelpful to assume that availability alone makes information equally ____7____ to everyone.

This does not require one universal typeface. It requires attention to use and a willingness to check an ____8____ against actual reading conditions. A choice can ____9____ the work's character while improving its practical clarity.

The result may be quiet: a reader follows the argument without stopping to admire the letters. Typography has supported the text ____10____ without becoming the subject of every glance. Its success is partly in making another activity possible.

After revision, a person could follow the sequence on ____8____ own without needing to know which unspoken custom belonged to which table.
